readerTitle: Two cheap rivals. Only one was a real threat.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (생활용품·건자재 매장, 가족 레스토랑) + 실제 연구 사례 (Christensen의 철강 미니밀)
insight: 싼 경쟁자가 무서운 이유는 가격이 아니라, 그 가격에서도 돈을 버는 다른 비용 구조와 내가 기꺼이 내주는 고객층이다.
misconception: 가격을 낮춘 경쟁자는 모두 같은 위협이고, 가장 싼 곳이 가장 위험하다. 수익성 낮은 고객을 내주는 것은 언제나 현명한 후퇴다.

sources.text: Christensen, C. M., & Raynor, M. E. (2003). The Innovator's Solution. Harvard Business School Press. (low-end vs new-market disruption 구분)
Christensen, C. M. (1997). The Innovator's Dilemma. Harvard Business School Press. (철강 미니밀 사례)
Lepore, J. (2014, June 23). The Disruption Machine. The New Yorker.
매장·레스토랑 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 'low-end disruption'이라는 구분이 Christensen & Raynor(2003) The Innovator's Solution에서 정리되었다는 점을 확인하세요.
미니밀 사례: 전기로로 고철을 녹이는 방식, 철근(rebar)에서 시작해 봉강·형강·이후 판재(sheet)로 올라간 순서는 Christensen의 서술을 따랐습니다. 시작 시기를 '1960s and 70s'로 넓게 적었으니 원문 연도와 대조하세요.
Jill Lepore의 2014년 New Yorker 비판 기사 제목·게재일과, 이론이 예측력보다 사후 설명에 강하다는 요지로 요약한 것이 적절한지 확인하세요.
매장의 15%·25% 할인, 800개 품목, 레스토랑의 30% 저렴·5분 제공 등은 모두 설명용 가상 수치입니다.

cards.title: Two cheap rivals. Only one was a real threat.
body: Two discount rivals open near a long-running home-supply store in the same month. Both charge less than it does.
One is gone within a year. The other, slowly and politely, starts taking the store's best customers.
The difference wasn't the price. It was what sat behind the price.

image.label: Two small shops opening beside one large store
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 가운데 오래된 대형 생활용품 매장, 양옆에 새로 문을 연 작은 매장 두 곳. 왼쪽 매장은 화려한 '15% OFF' 현수막, 오른쪽은 소박한 창고형 외관에 짧은 선반. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Which rival should worry you more?
body: You own a full-service home-supply store: wide range, expert staff, delivery. Two rivals open nearby.

**Store A** copies your format and runs 15% off everything, paid for by its owner's savings. **Store B** stocks only the 800 most common items, has no advice desk, rents a cheap warehouse and makes a profit at prices 25% below yours. Your bargain-hunting weekend customers like it.

options.text: Store A, because it discounts everything you sell
options.feedback: It hurts today, but Store A has your costs and lower prices. Every sale loses money, so it can only last as long as the savings do.

options.text: Store B, because it profits at a price you can't match
options.feedback: Right. Store B isn't running a promotion. It has a different cost model, and that can keep going and keep improving.

options.text: Neither. Your contractors and expert advice keep you safe
options.feedback: True for now: your most demanding customers stay. But that comfort is exactly what gives Store B room to start.

cards.title: The quiet rival climbed.
body: Store A's savings ran out in about a year. Prices went back up, then the doors closed.
Store B barely worried the owner. It took the customers buying cheap paint and hinges, the lowest-margin sales anyway. The owner dropped some of those lines and focused on contractors.
Then Store B added a trade counter. Then delivery. Each step up was small, and each one took customers the owner still wanted.

cards.title: Low-end disruption
body: **Low-end disruption** happens when a newcomer serves the least demanding customers with something *good enough*, using a business model that makes money at a price the leader can't match.

These customers are *overserved*: they pay for range, service or quality they don't use. The leader usually lets them go, because they're its least profitable customers. Clayton Christensen and Michael Raynor set out the idea in their 2003 book *The Innovator's Solution*.

image.label: A staircase: the newcomer climbs as the leader steps up
image.brief: 계단 인포그래픽. 아래 계단부터 'Basic', 'Mid', 'Demanding' 라벨. 작은 신생 매장 아이콘이 한 칸씩 올라오고, 큰 매장 아이콘은 매번 한 칸 위로 물러남. 화살표로 이동 방향 표시. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Steel mills that kept stepping back.
body: Christensen's best-known example is steel. Starting in the 1960s and 70s, minimills melted scrap in electric furnaces. That cost far less than running giant integrated mills, but early quality was only good enough for rebar, the low-grade steel inside concrete.
Big mills were glad to give up rebar, their worst-margin product. Minimills improved and moved up to bars, beams and later sheet steel. Each time, the big mills retreated to the next tier.
**Every retreat looked sensible.** Together, they shrank the big mills' market.

cards.title: Cheaper isn't enough. Look for three signs.
body: A low price alone is just competition. Low-end disruption needs all of these:
list: **Overserved customers:** some customers pay for more than they use
**A different cost model:** the newcomer profits at the low price, rather than surviving a promotion
**A leader happy to retreat:** the lost customers are ones the leader thinks it doesn't want
cards.callout: When all three hold, expect the newcomer to climb.
cards.softwareNote: A simple invoicing tool can win small firms that use a fraction of a big accounting suite's features. The suite maker often shrugs and chases bigger accounts, which gives the simple tool room to grow upward.

cards.title: Not every cheap rival climbs.
body: Some newcomers stay at the bottom. Better quality might wipe out their cost advantage, or the top customers may truly need what the leader offers.

The label is also overused. Critics, including historian Jill Lepore in a 2014 *New Yorker* essay, argue the theory explains the past better than it predicts the future. Treat the three signs as questions to investigate, not a verdict.

cards.title: Now it's a family restaurant.
body: You run a sit-down restaurant with waiters and a long menu. A counter-service spot opens nearby: eight dishes, order at the counter, food in five minutes, about 30% cheaper. It's profitable, and your weekday lunch crowd is drifting there.
What do you do?

options.feedback: Your waiters and long menu cost the same at any price. You'd lose money on every lunch while they keep making it.

options.text: Drop weekday lunch and focus on dinners and events
options.feedback: A sensible retreat that protects margins today. It also hands them a base to climb from, so watch for evening hours and catering.

options.text: Open a separate quick-lunch counter with its own short menu and lean staffing
options.feedback: You compete with a cost model built for the low price instead of forcing yours to stretch. It costs money and may eat some of your own lunch sales.

cards.softwareNote: The same move appears when a software company launches a separate, cheaper product with its own team and pricing, rather than discounting its main plan.

cards.title: Watch the business model behind a low price.
body: A cheap rival with your costs is a price war. A cheap rival with a different cost model, serving customers you overserve, may be the start of a climb.
**Try it today:** list the customers who use the least of what you offer. If someone served only them, cheaply and profitably, what would they add next?
